About: Worldline Length and Proper Time

Source

Lecture
9 — Proper Time
Simulation
Simulation 1 (guided inquiry): Worldline length and proper time
Concept
The straight (inertial) worldline between two events maximizes the proper time elapsed — opposite to Euclidean intuition about the "shortest path."
Serves
Define proper time as an invariant along a worldline; explain the geometric meaning of elapsed time in spacetime; relate proper time to physical clock measurements.
Inquiry
Predict which of two reunited travellers ages most (a third worldline is optional); construct each worldline and record proper time; rank them; optionally switch to S′ and check whether τ (vs Δt′) changes.
Misconception
"The traveller who took the longer path through space must have aged more — they covered more distance." Encoded as prediction option (a); rebuttal appears only when selected.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two travellers, one reunion

Let’s start with a story about two clocks. Two travellers leave together at E₁ and meet again at E₂. A goes straight, while B swings out through space and comes back. Whose own clock — whose proper time τ — do you think reads more at the reunion?

The τ totals are live now, so take a look: you can read them on the diagram and beside each traveller’s name.

2 · B's point of view

But wait — B could insist that it was A who moved away and came back. Between two inertial observers, time dilation is symmetric. So why do you think these two clocks disagree at all?

Look at the diagram: A runs from E₁ to E₂ as one unbroken segment, while B turns at its waypoint.

3 · One segment at a time

Now let’s zoom in on B. B’s journey is two straight segments, each with its own Δτ. Push B’s turning point further out in space, leaving E₁ and E₂ where they are. What do you think happens to those two Δτ values?

Try it: select B in the Worldline controls, then drag its amber turning point sideways — each Δτ falls, and the total τ_B with them.

4 · A second observer

Now let’s bring in someone new. A second observer glides past at speed v and describes the same two journeys, redrawing every worldline. Which numbers do you think that observer gets the same as we do?

Go ahead and switch the Frame to S′, then slide v/c: you’ll see the Δτ column hold while Δt′ moves.

5 · Maximal ageing

So here’s the big idea. Between two timelike-separated events the straight, inertial worldline records the greatest proper time; every excursion through space subtracts from it. That’s the twin paradox — B's clock reads less because B's worldline is bent — and τ, unlike coordinate time, is the same in every frame.

Proper time of a timelike segment

Δτ ≡ proper time = the time read by a clock carried along the segment. Natural units, c = 1.

Spacetime interval — signature (−,+)

ds² < 0 ⇒ timelike ⇒ real proper time, Δτ = √(−ds²)/c. Δx² enters ds² with the opposite sign to the time term, which is why detours shorten τ.

Total proper time along a worldline

The inertial (straight) worldline is the unique path that maximizes this sum.

Lorentz boost to S′  (γ ≡ 1/√(1−(v/c)²))

Coordinate time Δt′ is frame-dependent; proper time τ is invariant — equal in S and S′.

The Physics

Worldline length and proper time · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A clock carried along a path through spacetime reads the proper time τ of that path. This sim sends two travellers from one event to another along different worldlines, so you can compare their clocks and see what a clock's reading depends on.

What you'll learn

  • How a clock's reading along one straight segment is built from its time step and space step.
  • How the readings of different worldlines between the same two events compare, and what sets them.
  • How a worldline's total is built from its segments.
  • Which quantities change when a second observer describes the same journeys, and which do not.
Two worldlines join the same two events E₁ and E₂. Space x runs across, time ct runs up, and c = 1.

What's on screen

  • Blue line A: the straight worldline from E₁ to E₂.
  • Amber line B: a worldline with one kink at the amber dot, which you can drag.
  • Violet dots E₁ and E₂: the two shared events. They can be dragged too.
  • Dashed lines: the light cone of E₁. A clock's worldline has to stay steeper than these.
  • Proper time panel (sidebar): the clock reading τ of each worldline.
See itRun both travellers from E₁ to E₂ in the opening layout. Watch for: a marker riding up each worldline, from E₁ at the bottom to E₂ at the top.

03

Proper time comes from the interval

An event is a point (x, ct), and a worldline is the path a traveller takes through events. A clock carried along one straight segment reads

Δ(ct) is the segment's time step, Δx its space step, and c = 1.

This is the lectures' convention, signature (−, +): the time term is negative, so a timelike interval has Δs² < 0.

The interval in the lecture convention: timelike means Δs² < 0.

Some textbooks write the interval with the opposite overall sign, (+, −, −, −). The clock reading Δτ is the same either way; this course uses the lecture form above.

A clock can only follow a segment that stays steeper than the light cone, |Δx| < Δ(ct). Then Δs² is negative and Δτ is real. With Δx = 0 the clock stays at one place and Δτ = Δ(ct).

B's first leg in the opening layout: Δs² = −2.50² + 1.50² = −4.00, so Δτ = √4.00 = 2.00.
See itShow the segment table for B in the opening layout. Watch for: the table in the sidebar listing Δτ = 2.00 for both of B's legs.
04

Sideways steps shorten the clock reading

Hold Δ(ct) fixed and widen Δx. Δx² enters Δs² with a plus sign, so Δs² rises towards 0 and Δτ = √(−Δs²) falls. On paper the slanted segment is longer than the vertical one; on the clock it is shorter.

  • In S a segment with Δx/Δ(ct) = v/c has Δτ = Δ(ct)/γ, the familiar time dilation: S measures the moving clock running slow by γ.
  • B's legs in the opening layout have v = 0.60c, so γ = 1.25 and Δτ = 2.50 / 1.25 = 2.00.
  • With the kink at height ct = 2.5, moving it to x = 0, 1.50 and 2.40 gives each leg Δτ = 2.50, 2.00 and 0.70.
  • As |Δx| approaches Δ(ct), Δτ goes to 0. Light itself has Δτ = 0.
The same statement with v/c: time dilation, as measured in S.
One clock over Δ(ct) = 5 at different speeds: the closer to the light cone, the less it records.
See itSlide B's kink outward from x = 0 to x = 2.40. Watch for: both Δτ entries for B in the sidebar table falling from 2.50 to 0.70.
05

Proper time adds up along a path

A bent worldline is a chain of straight segments, and its clock reads the sum of their Δτ.

When every segment is timelike and runs forward in time, as the sim keeps them, no bent path beats the straight one.

This is the triangle inequality turned round: in Δs² the space steps carry the opposite sign to the time steps, so two sides of a spacetime triangle sum to less than the third. In the opening layout τA = 5.00, while B reads 2.00 + 2.00 = 4.00. A second bend costs more: the sim's worldline C reads 2.88.

B's kink, x

This slider moves the sim too. The sim stops the kink before a leg reaches the light cone.

Put the kink at x = 0 and B lies along A, so the readings agree.

See itAdd worldline C, which bends twice. Watch for: the clock readouts ranking A first, B second and C last.
06

Every observer agrees on proper time

A second observer S′ moves along x at speed v relative to S, with β = v/c and γ = 1/√(1 − β²). The sim redraws every worldline in S′ using the boost below, with c = 1.

The sim's Δt′ column is Δ(ct′) with c = 1.

The boost mixes the time and space steps, so Δt′ changes with β. It also keeps Δs² = −Δ(ct)² + Δx² fixed, so Δτ = √(−Δs²) does not change.

  • At β = 0.50 (γ = 1.155), B's legs take Δt′ = 2.02 and 3.75 in place of 2.50 and 2.50, yet each still reads Δτ = 2.00.
  • A's Δt′ is 5.77 in S′, and its clock still reads 5.00. In the opening layout A is at rest in S, so τA happens to equal S's coordinate time there.
  • Every observer sees the same kink in B's worldline. A and B cannot be swapped by changing frame.
See itSwitch to S′ and sweep v/c from 0 to 0.6, then to −0.6. Watch for: the two Δt′ values moving, while both Δτ values stay at 2.00.
07

Where it matters

  • Cosmic-ray muons. A muon's own clock gives it a lifetime of about 2.2 μs. At 0.999c, γ = 22.4, so in the ground frame it lasts about 49 μs and travels roughly 15 km. Without dilation that distance would be under 1 km.
  • GPS. Satellite clocks lose about 7 μs a day to their motion and gain about 45 μs a day from weaker gravity, a net 38 μs a day. Left uncorrected, that would put positions off by roughly 11 km a day.
  • Flown clocks. In 1971, Hafele and Keating flew atomic clocks around the world on airliners. Compared with a clock that stayed home, they differed by tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, as motion and gravity together predict.
  • The twin paradox. This is the same picture: the travelling twin's worldline is bent between two meetings, so that twin's clock records less.
Go deeper: why straight lines extremise proper time
  • For a free particle, the worldline that makes the total proper time stationary is the straight one. In special relativity that stationary value is a maximum, so inertial motion is the path of maximal ageing.
  • The same principle carries into general relativity: a freely falling clock follows the worldline that extremises its proper time, which is why GPS clock rates are worked out from the proper time along each satellite's orbit.
08

Summary

In one line. A clock reads the interval along its own worldline, so its reading depends on the path and not only on the endpoints; the straight path records the most, and every observer agrees on each reading.

Key points

  • Along one segment, Δs² = −Δ(ct)² + Δx² and Δτ = √(−Δs²), with c = 1.
  • At fixed Δ(ct), a wider Δx gives a smaller Δτ.
  • A worldline's total is the sum of its segments' Δτ, and a bent path between two events records less than the straight one.
  • Boosting to S′ changes Δt′ but not Δτ.

Common mix-ups

  • "The path through space that is longer on the diagram must take more time." In Δs² the space step has the opposite sign to the time step, so the longer-looking path records less.
  • "B ages less because B was the one moving." Motion is relative. What separates the travellers is straight versus bent.
  • "Δτ depends on which frame you compute it in." It does not. Only the coordinate time Δt′ changes under a boost.

Things to try on your own

  • Drag E₂ to (2, 5) with B's kink at (1.5, 2.5), and read both clocks. Check τA = √(−Δs²) = √21 ≈ 4.58 by hand.
  • Switch to S′ and set v/c = −0.50. Compare B's two Δt′ with those at +0.50.
  • Show worldline C and drag W₂ and W₃ onto A's line. Watch τC climb towards τA.
